title: Model catalog tiebreaker & bench-sprint kickoff

Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-09
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~57 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Liam (CTO), Rina (Lead ML), Marcus (Platform)

Auto-summary (auto-gen): Redwood demo of catalog shortlist and bench plan; customer concerned about latency and private deployment.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check-in, can you hear me okay?
[00:04] Liam: Yep, loud and clear.
[00:06] Maya: Cool. I'm Maya, AE on the account, with Ethan from our SE team. We're gonna run through the two shortlisted model families and then sketch the bench-sprint to break the tie. Rina, Marcus, anything we should add to agenda?
[00:20] Rina: No, that's perfect. Main thing for us is confirm which model gives better cost/latency tradeoff for our chat scoring pipeline — and make sure it plays nice with our VPC + KMS setup.
[00:32] Ethan: Great. I'll start with the compatibility matrix view in the catalog so folks see where the models differ on kernel mapping, quantization readiness, and sequence length perf.

[00:45] [Screen share starts — faint typing noises] 
[01:00] Ethan: Alright, in the catalog here you can see the two families — one is an opt-style open model, the other is a llama-derivative — labelled family A and family B in our notes. Family A has a lower token cost in fp16 but the kernel map currently uses a different matmul path on A100 vs the T4 family. Family B is more friendly to int8 quantization and has an optimized attention kernel on Ampere.
[01:29] Rina: When you say "kernel map" can you show where that lives in the console? I wanna see which hardware we should plan for.
[01:36] Ethan: Yep, under the model details there's a compatibility matrix — shows supported devices, recommended quant profiles, and typical latency at batch sizes 1/4/8 for 512 tokens. Note these are representative; we always recommend running a short bench with your prompt shapes.
[01:50] Marcus: Quick question — our infra is VPC-only for inference, we can't route through public endpoints. Can Redwood Dedicated sit behind our VPC peering or do we need Private?
[02:02] Maya: Good question. For VPC-only restrictions you have two options: Redwood Private (customer-managed control plane in your VPC) or Dedicated with a private network peering option. We'll send the networking checklist, but from a bench perspective we can do an initial sprint using a private tunnel if needed.
[02:18] Liam: Are there any caveats around KMS — we use HashiCorp Vault for our keys.
[02:24] Ethan: We support bring-your-own-KMS including Vault via our KMS integration layer; for Private deployments you can also use HSM-backed keys. We'll include integration notes in the security pack.
[02:33] Rina: Cool. Back to the models — we care about P95 for user-facing latency, but also throughput for batch scoring. Family A looks lower cost on paper, but family B's int8 gives a better p95 in some of your benchmarks?
[02:45] Ethan: Exactly. In our catalog the sample bench shows family A has better median tokens/sec at small batch sizes, but family B's quantized path has better p95 at scale because of improved memory bandwidth utilization. There's also cache behavior differences — family A benefits more from prefix kv cache for repeated context.
[03:05] [03:10] Maya: To make the tiebreaker clear we'll run a 3-day bench-sprint: two parallel bench tracks for the two families, using your canonical prompt set, capturing p50/p95/p99, token cost, and failure/retry behavior under simulated spikes.
[03:24] Liam: Sounds good. What's the infra footprint for each during the sprint? We need to budget GPU hours.
[03:29] Ethan: For the sprint we'll provide recommended instance sizes in the bench template. Roughly: small pilot uses 1x A100 or equivalent for each model track with a short warm-up, then scale to 2 nodes for throughput runs. We'll provide a cost estimate range in the spreadsheet.
[03:44] Rina: Are you planning to use continuous batching during the bench? Our production pipeline uses micro-batches with variable sizes.
[03:51] Ethan: We'll simulate your batch distribution. Redwood Optimize can suggest batching profiles — but for fairness in the sprint we'll run both a latency-optimized profile (batch=1, lower timeout) and a throughput-optimized profile (batch up to 8, 50ms batching window).
[04:06] Marcus: Is there an easy way to capture kernel-level metrics? We have a performance SW engineer who likes to dig into flop/s and mem-bound stats.
[04:14] Ethan: Yes, we can surface serving runtime metrics — per-kernel time breakdown, GPU utilization, memory pressure, and KV cache hit rates — we'll include a short SE notebook to parse those logs. Some field names might be slightly different in the export; the console visualizes the hot paths.
[04:30] [04:35] Liam: Okay, two administrative questions: SOC2 and data retention — we need to ensure PII is not stored; and second, can we get an NDA before we share some of our prompt set?
[04:45] Maya: We have SOC2 Type II; we'll attach the compliance pack. For prompt-level confidentiality we can sign an NDA — I'll loop legal and send a one-week turnaround NDA. Retention-wise, we can configure zero retention on your customer routes or route logs into your VPC.
[05:01] Rina: Great. Also, are there any model license issues with the llama-derivative family for commercial use? We need to confirm licensing clearance before committing.
[05:10] Ethan: We'll include model license metadata in the bench packet — some open families have specific attribution or non-commercial clauses, but our catalog flags those. For the family B variant we've vetted for commercial permissiveness but we'll double-check and put the exact license text in the docs.
[05:25] [05:30] Rina: Awesome. On the bench details: we want to run 512 token contexts and a separate 2k token long form run to test AP memory usage — is that supported?
[05:37] Ethan: Absolutely. The runtime supports variable context lengths; we'll include both 512 and 2048 token runs in the template. Note some quantized kernels reduce max context or change perf curve; we'll call that out per-model.
[05:48] Marcus: For the private deployment, how do rollouts look? If we pin to a model version and then need to fallback, what's the policy?
[05:56] Maya: Rollouts can be configured in the console: canary %s, A/B with automatic fallback to a lower-latency variant, or region fallback. For Dedicated/Private you'll get the same semantics but your ops team controls the pinning.
[06:10] [06:15] Liam: One more: competitor question — we looked at Vertex and Anthropic; what does Redwood bring that the others don't for this sort of bench?
[06:22] Ethan: Two main things: first, catalog-level compatibility metadata + kernel mapping so you know which model variants actually run well on your target GPU; second, the Optimize toolkit that recommends batching/quant profiles tied to unit economics — so you get actionable knobs, not just raw throughput numbers.
[06:39] Rina: Any pitfalls you commonly see when customers compare medians vs p95?
[06:44] Ethan: Yeah, medians can hide tail latency spikes caused by cache misses or large context crossing kernel thresholds. We instrument p95/p99 and run synthetic spike tests. For example, some models jump latency beyond token 1024 because the attention kernel switches. That's in the compatibility notes.
[07:02] [07:10] Maya: Ok, let's go through the bench-template columns quickly — we'll share this after the call.
[07:15] Ethan: Column list: model family/version, hardware used, quantization profile, batch config, prompt set id, run type (latency/throughput/long-context), p50/p95/p99, cost per 1k tokens, GPU hours consumed, error rate, notes on kernel behavior.
[07:31] Rina: For cost we prefer token-based estimate and GPU-hour estimate — both.
[07:34] Ethan: We'll provide both.
[07:36] Liam: For the bench sprint timeline, you suggested 3 days — can you spell who does what?
[07:40] Maya: Day 0: infra prep and confirm prompts; Day 1: latency runs; Day 2: throughput + stress tests; Day 3: analysis and recommendation. Redwood SE runs and collects logs, customer validates results. We'll keep a shared sheet.
[07:56] Marcus: If we discover a kernel mismatch that leads to poor perf on our GPU choice, can you recompile or is that on your roadmap?
[08:04] Ethan: Our runtime picks kernels automatically but we also have kernel tuning options. For enterprise pilots we can run a quick kernel selection pass and adjust threading/tiling parameters; that's part of what the SE bench includes, though deep kernel development would be longer-term.
[08:20] [08:25] Rina: I'd like a short spike to see family B with int8 on our target instance — is that feasible during the sprint?
[08:31] Ethan: Yes, we'll make that one of the tasks.
[08:34] Liam: Great. Any red flags from cost perspective?
[08:37] Maya: Not yet. We'll share ballpark pricing ranges and show sensitivity to batch size and quantization. Also note, routing policies can reduce cost by falling back to cheaper variants on non-critical requests.
[08:50] Rina: On the sample prompts — some are structured JSON tool calls, some plain text. Will that affect bench outcomes?
[08:58] Ethan: It can. Structured output with tool calls often changes tokenization patterns and leads to different average token lengths. We recommend splitting prompt sets by type so you get apples-to-apples comparisons.
[09:10] [09:15] Liam: Ok looks like we're aligned. Let's confirm the immediate deliverables. Maya?
[09:20] Maya: I'll send: bench spreadsheet, high-level pricing ranges, compliance pack (SOC2), and an NDA template. Ethan will send the SE bench notebook and kernel notes. Customer to send prompt set and confirm infra details. We'll aim to kick off the sprint on 2027-02-16.
[09:40] Rina: That timeline works for us, pending Marcus confirming VPC/KMS by the 15th.
[09:46] Marcus: I'll try to confirm earlier, but 15th is safe.
[09:50] Liam: Anything else?
[09:52] Ethan: Two small items — one, we'll include a recommended fallback model variant for each family in case of memory pressure; two, we'll log any license red flags per model.
[10:03] Rina: Perfect.
[10:05] [10:10] Maya: Thanks all. We'll follow up with the materials.
[10:13] Liam: Thanks, talk soon.

[10:30] End of recording.
